one_liner: Java ziggurat normal sampler (GSL port); about 6-8x faster than polar-method Random/ThreadLocalRandom.nextGaussian on JDK 17.
what_it_does: A small Java 11+ library (Maven Central org.cicirello:ziggurat) with one useful class, ZigguratGaussian, whose static methods return N(0,1) or N(0, sigma) doubles. You pass a java.util.Random (so SecureRandom too) or SplittableRandom, or call the no-argument form, which uses ThreadLocalRandom.current(). It is not a subclass or wrapper, so call sites change from r.nextGaussian() to ZigguratGaussian.nextGaussian(r). A PolarGaussian class with the same API is included only as a comparison point.
how_it_is_fast: It replaces the Marsaglia polar method (two uniforms, a rejection loop and a log plus sqrt per pair) with the Marsaglia-Tsang ziggurat as simplified in Jochen Voss's GSL gauss.c: 128 layers, an exponential-wedge tail, and precomputed ytab/ktab/wtab tables. The common path is one 32-bit nextInt() split into sign (1 bit), layer (7 bits) and a 24-bit integer j, an integer compare j < ktab[i] and one multiply, with no transcendental call; StrictMath.exp/log run only on the rare wedge and tail branches. Port changes over GSL: one nextInt() instead of two RNG calls, and multiplication by a precomputed 1/R instead of division.
when_to_use: Java code that draws many Gaussians from java.util.Random or SecureRandom on any JDK: those classes still use the synchronized polar method (103.0 vs 17.4 ns/op for Random in the JDK 17 JMH run).
ThreadLocalRandom on JDK 11 through 25: its nextGaussian is the inherited polar method there (88.8 vs 10.9 ns/op on JDK 17).
Any of the legacy generators, SplittableRandom included, on JDK 11 to 16, where the JDK has no ziggurat at all (README table).

Gaussian-mutation-heavy evolutionary algorithms and simulations that must stay on Java 11 and cannot adopt the Java 17 RandomGenerator API; the library was written to speed up a parallel genetic algorithm.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ projects: it is pure Java with no native or C ABI; this catalog's C/C++ ziggurat entries (cauldron random.h, normaldist-benchmark, EigenRand) are the comparable choices.

SplittableRandom or any java.util.random.RandomGenerator on JDK 17+: the JDK's own McFarland modified ziggurat is faster (8.93 vs 10.09 ns/op for SplittableRandom; wrapping ThreadLocalRandom as a RandomGenerator gave 10.39 vs 10.90 ns/op), and the author's report says the same.

ThreadLocalRandom on JDK 26 and later: OpenJDK commit 8372134 (master, 2025-11-27) made ThreadLocalRandom.nextGaussian call RandomSupport.computeNextGaussian, the modified ziggurat, so the 8x gap measured on JDK 17 should be gone there (inference from the JDK source; not benchmarked).
Code that must reproduce existing seeded runs: the output sequence and the number of RNG draws per sample differ from r.nextGaussian(), so fixed-seed experiments change.
Projects that cannot take GPL-3.0-or-later code (the Java source carries the GSL GPL lineage; there is no permissive variant).

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (JUnit Jupiter for tests only)
integration.min_toolchain: Java 11 (pom.xml maven.compiler.release 11; jars built with OpenJDK 25 targeting 11)
integration.thread_safety: Static methods over immutable final tables, so safety follows the generator you pass: the no-argument form uses ThreadLocalRandom.current() and is safe per thread; Random is thread-safe but shared instances contend; SplittableRandom must not be shared across threads.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same N(0,1) contract and Random/SplittableRandom/ThreadLocalRandom sources, but it is a static utility (no override of nextGaussian), so every call site must be rewritten and the random sequence changes.

gotchas: Easy to bypass by accident: r.nextGaussian() still compiles and still runs the slow JDK method; the source comments name this as the drawback of the static-utility design.

Fast-path resolution is limited by the 24-bit j: x = j * wtab[i], so each layer yields at most 2^24 distinct magnitudes (the GSL design), coarser than a 53-bit double; fine for simulation and evolutionary algorithms, worth knowing for tail-sensitive statistics.
Wedge and tail use StrictMath.exp and StrictMath.log (bit-reproducible across JVMs, slower than Math); they run only in the rare rejection branches.

The repo says the code has been absorbed into cicirello/rho-mu (GPL-3.0); rho-mu 5.x needs Java 25, 2.x-4.x need Java 17 and 1.x Java 11, so pick that library if you want the same sampler plus RandomGenerator wrappers.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only in Java code still on Random, SecureRandom or (before JDK 26) ThreadLocalRandom, or on JDK 11-16; for C++ the catalogued cauldron random.h ziggurat (4.0 vs 8.9 ns per float sample over std::normal_distribution) or EigenRand's vectorized normals are the relevant choices, and dqrng covers R/C++ users.
verified_claims_summary: One JMH 1.37 run on OpenJDK 17.0.2 (1 thread, 1 fork, 5x10 s warmup and measurement, Windows host, CPU not stated) measured average ns per sample: Random 103.04 built-in vs 17.39 ziggurat (about 5.9x, derived from page data), ThreadLocalRandom 88.77 vs 10.90 (about 8.1x, derived), but SplittableRandom 8.93 built-in vs 10.09 ziggurat and ThreadLocalRandom-as-RandomGenerator 10.39 vs 10.90, so the JDK 17 modified ziggurat wins wherever it is reachable. Benchmark source and raw output are public; the accompanying arXiv report (2405.19493) was seen only as a search snippet, which states the same conclusion.
status_note: Active in name only (v1.1.2 of 2026-07-08 is a CI-only release, 0 open issues, 10 stars, recent commits are dependency bumps) because the author has moved the code into rho-mu; GPL-3.0-or-later, a single ~750-line source file, on Maven Central.
